method: For each corner it takes the best low-cost fix the evidence supports without a site visit (brief.SUPPORTED: measured in this city, the record FHWA cites, or the median of national studies whose conditions the record shows), and keeps apart the larger "textbook" estimate that would need a site check or that the city's own record contradicts. One fix per corner, never added together at a corner (the Highway Safety Manual's simple method does not allow stacking).
caveats: Estimates use the Highway Safety Manual's simple method; a qualified engineer must review each fix.
One fix per corner; totals add corners, so a crash near two corners can count twice.
The regression-to-the-mean factor is measured within the listed corners, so it is a lower bound on that effect where the corners were themselves picked by the same records.

letter.subject: 48 high-crash intersections on your roads
letter.body: In the 5 years of public police crash records up to 2026-10-31, the 48 high-crash intersections in Seattle where we presume you are responsible for at least one of the roads had 3,497 injury crashes. At 48 of them, a low-cost fix the evidence supports would avoid about 72.2 crashes a year, worth about $24.7 million a year at the U.S. DOT's values. The table lists each intersection, the fix and the evidence behind it. We ask for a safety review at each intersection and for the fixes listed, and a reply on which you will take up.
